content: 1. Specific feeding strategies for premature infants include the use of modified animal milk. During the rehabilitation phase of treatment, milk options are similar to those used in earlier phases. Feeding protocols are defined by the duration of stabilization and transition phases, and feeding routes include supplementary suckling (SS), cup feeding, or spoon feeding. 2. In control groups, breast milk (if accessible) or breast milk substitutes (BMS) are used. Primary outcomes measured include mortality, while secondary outcomes include weight gain, diarrhea, restoration of effective exclusive or sustained breastfeeding, time to recovery, length gain, nutritional recovery, and recurrence of malnutrition. 3. The setting for these interventions is inpatient care. 4. Inclusion criteria for studies reviewed include both observational and randomized studies (due to the limited number of randomized studies), infants under 6 months of age, studies reporting treatment details and outcomes, and studies in any language. 5. Exclusion criteria did not eliminate studies based on poor methodological quality, but the quality of each study was rated, documented, and interpreted accordingly. 6. Search terms for therapeutic feeding strategies during stabilization, transition, and rehabilitation phases included terms related to infant nutrition disorders, wasting, malnutrition, and milk. Specific questions addressed the safest and most effective feeding strategies, protocols, and modes of therapeutic feeding. 7. Guidelines from 36 countries were identified, with 78% originating from Africa. Of these, 81% had specific sections addressing infants under 6 months with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). The space devoted to this age group ranged from 2% to 19% of total page counts, with a mean of 8%. 8. All 29 guidelines recommended inpatient care for infants under 6 months. Over half (55%) mentioned a dedicated breastfeeding corner or similar separate location for treating these infants. 9. The primary treatment aim in 83% of guidelines was improving or re-establishing exclusive breastfeeding (EBF). Core interventions included supplementary suckling (SS) in 97% of cases, with one guideline mentioning alternative feeding methods like cups, syringes, or nasogastric tubes. Kangaroo care was specifically noted in 3% of guidelines for nursing infants under 6 months. 10. Vitamin A supplementation was recommended in 86% of guidelines, with most suggesting a dose of 50,000 IU upon admission for infants under 6 months. Some guidelines exempted edematous SAM cases or recommended supplementation at week 4 or discharge instead. 11. First-line antibiotics were recommended in 86% of guidelines, with amoxicillin being the most common choice. Dosage regimens varied widely, with some guidelines recommending combinations of amoxicillin and gentamicin. Second-line antibiotics were specified in 21% of guidelines, with gentamicin being the most common. 12. Antimalarial treatments were not explicitly recommended for infants under 6 months, though some guidelines referred to national protocols or specified that antimalarials should not be given to infants weighing less than 5 kg. 13. Iron supplementation was recommended in 79% of guidelines, often via ferrous sulfate administered through F-100 therapeutic milk. Most guidelines advised delaying iron supplementation until the infant showed improvement or was suckling well. 14. For infants with breastfeeding potential, 90% of guidelines recommended breastfeeding every three hours for at least 20 minutes, with additional feeds if the infant was willing. Breast milk substitutes (BMS) were suggested in some cases, typically given 30–60 minutes after breastfeeding. 15. During the stabilization phase, 97% of guidelines recommended using F-100 diluted (F-100d) as the primary BMS, with F-75 used for edematous SAM cases. Feeding frequency was typically eight times per day, with a volume of 130–135 ml/kg/day, equating to 100 kcal/kg/day. 16. In the rehabilitation phase, F-100d was gradually reduced as the infant transitioned to exclusive breastfeeding. Most guidelines recommended stopping BMS entirely if the infant continued to gain more than 10 g/day during this phase. 17. Definitions of cure varied, with some guidelines specifying weight gain thresholds (e.g., 15–20% of original weight) or weight-for-length (W/L) z-scores. Discharge criteria often included sustained weight gain on exclusive breastfeeding. 18. Preparation for discharge included ensuring immunizations were up-to-date, counseling mothers on health and nutrition, and providing play therapy or stimulation for infants. Maternal diet recommendations included consuming at least 2 liters of water and 2,500 kcal per day, along with vitamin A supplementation. 19. Psychosocial support for mothers was emphasized in 93% of guidelines, with recommendations for reassurance, attentiveness, and addressing maternal depression or trauma. 20. HIV-related considerations included recognizing lactose intolerance in HIV-positive children, following international guidelines for prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and providing antiretroviral therapy (ART) and antibiotics like amoxicillin and co-trimoxazole. Heat treatment of breast milk for HIV-positive mothers was mentioned in one guideline. 21. Follow-up care for infants was addressed in most guidelines, though specific details were not provided in this excerpt.
